questions.target: Inference for the slope of a regression line
questions.answer: \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) (no linear relationship). \(H_a:\beta_1\neq0\) (there is a linear relationship). Test statistic: \(t=\frac{b_1-0}{SE_{b_1}}=\frac{6.2}{1.1}\approx5.64\).

questions.q: State the four conditions (sometimes remembered as LINER: Linear, Independent, Normal, Equal variance, Random) required for valid inference about a regression slope.
questions.answer: (1) Linear: the true relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is linear. (2) Independent: individual observations are independent of each other. (3) Normal: for any fixed \(x\)-value, the responses \(y\) vary according to a normal distribution. (4) Equal variance: the standard deviation of \(y\) is the same for all values of \(x\) (no fanning pattern in the residuals). Additionally, data should come from a properly randomized design or random sample.
questions.explanation: (1) Linear: the true relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is linear. (2) Independent: individual observations are independent of each other. (3) Normal: for any fixed \(x\)-value, the responses \(y\) vary according to a normal distribution. (4) Equal variance: the standard deviation of \(y\) is the same for all values of \(x\) (no fanning pattern in the residuals). Additionally, data should come from a properly randomized design or random sample.

questions.q: A sample of \(n=300\) gives \(\hat p=0.49\). Construct a 99% confidence interval for the population proportion (\(z^*=2.576\)).
Explain the difference between a chi-square test of independence and a chi-square test of homogeneity, even though both use the same formula and table structure.
questions.answer: A test of independence uses a single sample and asks whether two categorical variables measured on the same individuals are associated. A test of homogeneity compares the distribution of a single categorical variable across two or more separate populations or groups (e.g. comparing the distribution of preferred learning style between two different schools) — the calculation and table setup are identical, but the sampling design and the question being asked differ.
questions.explanation: A test of independence uses a single sample and asks whether two categorical variables measured on the same individuals are associated. A test of homogeneity compares the distribution of a single categorical variable across two or more separate populations or groups (e.g. comparing the distribution of preferred learning style between two different schools) — the calculation and table setup are identical, but the sampling design and the question being asked differ.

questions.q: A genetics experiment expects offspring to appear in a 9:3:3:1 ratio across four phenotype categories, based on 160 total offspring observed. Find the expected count for each category, and briefly describe what the chi-square goodness-of-fit test would examine using these expected counts.
questions.target: Computing expected counts for a chi-square test
questions.answer: Total ratio parts: \(9+3+3+1=16\). Expected counts: \(\frac{9}{16}(160)=90\), \(\frac{3}{16}(160)=30\), \(\frac{3}{16}(160)=30\), \(\frac{1}{16}(160)=10\). The chi-square goodness-of-fit test would compare these expected counts to the actual observed counts in each category, computing \(\chi^2=\sum\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}\) to assess whether the observed offspring distribution is consistent with the predicted 9:3:3:1 genetic ratio.
questions.explanation: Total ratio parts: \(9+3+3+1=16\). Expected counts: \(\frac{9}{16}(160)=90\), \(\frac{3}{16}(160)=30\), \(\frac{3}{16}(160)=30\), \(\frac{1}{16}(160)=10\). The chi-square goodness-of-fit test would compare these expected counts to the actual observed counts in each category, computing \(\chi^2=\sum\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}\) to assess whether the observed offspring distribution is consistent with the predicted 9:3:3:1 genetic ratio.

questions.q: A study examines the relationship between hours of sleep per night (\(x\)) and reaction time in milliseconds (\(y\)) for 30 participants, finding a regression slope \(b_1=-8.5\) with standard error \(SE_{b_1}=2.3\). State the hypotheses for testing whether more sleep is associated with a significant decrease in reaction time (a one-sided test), compute the test statistic, and interpret the sign of the slope in context.
questions.target: Computing expected counts for a chi-square test
questions.answer: \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) (no linear relationship). \(H_a:\beta_1<0\) (more sleep is associated with decreasing reaction time). The negative slope indicates that, in this sample, reaction time tends to decrease (improve) as hours of sleep increase — consistent with the idea that more sleep is associated with faster reaction times.

questions.q: Eight patients with chronic insomnia try a new relaxation therapy. Their sleep duration (hours/night) is measured before and after 4 weeks of therapy: Patient differences \(d = \mathrm{After} - \mathrm{Before}\) yield \(\bar{x}_d = 1.25\mathrm{\ hours}\) and \(s_d = 0.80\mathrm{\ hours}\). Assuming normality of differences, test whether the therapy significantly increased sleep at \(\alpha = 0.01\).
questions.answer: 1. Method Choice: Paired data measured on the same 8 patients \(\Rightarrow\) Paired \(t\)-test on differences. 2. Hypotheses: \(H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad \mathrm{vs.} \quad H_a: \mu_d > 0 \quad (\alpha = 0.01),\) where \(\mu_d\) is the true mean difference in sleep duration (After minus Before). 3. Test Statistic & p-value: \(t = \frac{\bar{x}_d - 0}{s_d / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.25 - 0}{0.80 / \sqrt{8}} = \frac{1.25}{0.2828} \approx 4.42 \quad (df = 8 - 1 = 7).\) With \(df = 7\), \(P(T > 4.42) \approx 0.0015\). 4. Conclusion: Because \(\mathrm{p-value} = 0.0015 < \alpha = 0.01\), we reject \(H_0\). There is convincing statistical evidence that the relaxation therapy significantly increased sleep duration in patients.
questions.explanation: 1. Method Choice: Paired data measured on the same 8 patients \(\Rightarrow\) Paired \(t\)-test on differences. 2. Hypotheses: \(H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad \mathrm{vs.} \quad H_a: \mu_d > 0 \quad (\alpha = 0.01),\) where \(\mu_d\) is the true mean difference in sleep duration (After minus Before). 3. Test Statistic & p-value: \(t = \frac{\bar{x}_d - 0}{s_d / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.25 - 0}{0.80 / \sqrt{8}} = \frac{1.25}{0.2828} \approx 4.42 \quad (df = 8 - 1 = 7).\) With \(df = 7\), \(P(T > 4.42) \approx 0.0015\). 4. Conclusion: Because \(\mathrm{p-value} = 0.0015 < \alpha = 0.01\), we reject \(H_0\). There is convincing statistical evidence that the relaxation therapy significantly increased sleep duration in patients.

questions.q: A study investigates the effectiveness of a new teaching method by comparing the test scores of students who used the new method versus those who used the traditional method. The results are summarized in a two-way table. If the table has \(4\) rows and \(3\) columns, what is the degrees of freedom (df) for a chi-square test of homogeneity?
questions.answer: For a chi-square test of homogeneity or independence with a two-way table, the degrees of freedom (df) are calculated using the formula: \(\mathrm{df} = (r-1)(c-1)\), where \(r\) is the number of rows and \(c\) is the number of columns. In this case, the number of rows is \(r = 4\) and the number of columns is \(c = 3\). Substituting these values into the formula: \(\mathrm{df} = (4-1)(3-1) = (3)(2) = 6\). Therefore, the degrees of freedom are 6.
questions.explanation: For a chi-square test of homogeneity or independence with a two-way table, the degrees of freedom (df) are calculated using the formula: \(\mathrm{df} = (r-1)(c-1)\), where \(r\) is the number of rows and \(c\) is the number of columns. In this case, the number of rows is \(r = 4\) and the number of columns is \(c = 3\). Substituting these values into the formula: \(\mathrm{df} = (4-1)(3-1) = (3)(2) = 6\). Therefore, the degrees of freedom are 6.

questions.q: A pharmaceutical company is investigating the efficacy of a new drug to reduce blood pressure. They want to design a randomized controlled experiment. Participants will be recruited from a specific patient population. To ensure generalizability and account for potential confounding factors, the researchers decide to stratify the participants by age group (Under 40, 40-60, Over 60) and by the severity of their hypertension (Mild, Moderate, Severe). If there are 150 participants in total and an equal number of participants are to be assigned to each treatment group (Drug A, Drug B, Placebo), and the number of participants in each stratum is proportional to the expected prevalence in the general population, how many participants would be allocated to the stratum 'Under 40' and 'Mild' hypertension if the proportion of individuals in this stratum is 0.08?
questions.answer: The problem requires calculating the number of participants in a specific stratum within a larger experimental design. The total number of participants is 150. The participants are stratified by age group and hypertension severity. The proportion of individuals in the stratum 'Under 40' and 'Mild' hypertension is given as 0.08. To find the number of participants in this stratum, we multiply the total number of participants by the proportion of this stratum. Number of participants in 'Under 40' and 'Mild' stratum = Total participants × Proportion of stratum Number of participants = 150 × 0.08 Number of participants = 12 This calculation directly addresses the number of participants within a specific stratum, which is a key aspect of experimental design and sampling strategies. The information about the number of treatment groups and equal assignment to each treatment group is extraneous to the calculation of the stratum size based on its proportion.

questions.q: In the standard \((x,y)\) coordinate plane below, the graph of the quadratic function \(f(x) = 9 - x^2\) and the line \(g(x) = x + 3\) intersect at points \(A\) and \(B\), where \(A\) has a negative \(x\)-coordinate and \(B\) has a positive \(x\)-coordinate. Point \(C\) is the vertex of the parabola \(y = f(x)\). What is the area, in square coordinate units, of \(\Delta  ABC\)?
questions.answer: To find the area of \(\Delta  ABC\), we first determine the coordinates of its three vertices: \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\). 1. **Vertex \(C\)**: The function \(f(x) = 9 - x^2\) is a downward-opening parabola with its maximum at \(x = 0\). \(f(0) = 9 - 0^2 = 9\), so the vertex is \(C(0, 9)\). 2. **Intersection Points \(A\) and \(B\)**: Set \(f(x) = g(x)\): $9 - x^2 = x + 3\( Rearrange into standard quadratic form: \)x^2 + x - 6 = 0\( Factor the quadratic equation: \)(x + 3)(x - 2) = 0\( Thus, the \)x\(-coordinates of the intersection points are \)x = -3\( and \)x = 2\(. - For \)x = -3\(: \)y = g(-3) = -3 + 3 = 0\(, giving point \)A(-3, 0)\(. - For \)x = 2\(: \)y = g(2) = 2 + 3 = 5\(, giving point \)B(2, 5)\(. 3. **Area of \)\Delta  ABC\(**: Using the coordinate geometry area formula (Shoelace formula) for vertices \)(-3, 0)\(, \)(2, 5)\(, and \)(0, 9)\(: \)\mathrm{Area} = \frac{1}{2} |x_A(y_B - y_C) + x_B(y_C - y_A) + x_C(y_A - y_B)|\( Substitute the coordinates: \)\mathrm{Area} = \frac{1}{2} |-3(5 - 9) + 2(9 - 0) + 0(0 - 5)|\( \)\mathrm{Area} = \frac{1}{2} |-3(-4) + 2(9) + 0| = \frac{1}{2} |12 + 18| = \frac{1}{2}(30) = 15\( Alternatively, enclosing \)\Delta  ABC\( in a bounding rectangle with horizontal span from \)x = -3\( to \)x = 2\( (width 5) and vertical span from \)y = 0\( to \)y = 9\( (height 9) gives a total box area of \)5 \times 9 = 45\(. Subtracting the three surrounding right triangles gives \)45 - \frac{1}{2}(5)(5) - \frac{1}{2}(2)(4) - \frac{1}{2}(3)(9) = 45 - 12.5 - 4 - 13.5 = 15\(. Common errors include forgetting the factor of \)\frac{1}{2}$ (yielding 30) or multiplying the horizontal width by the total height and dividing by 2 without adjusting for the non-right shape (yielding 22.5).
